title: Lost: Stay or Go?
description: How people really get lost, why they walk in circles, and when to stay put
tryIt: On your next walk somewhere new, stop at each junction, point to where you started, then check your guess on a map.

concepts.title: How it works: why you walk in circles
concepts.contentHtml:
The mist comes down on the moor at four o'clock. Ten minutes ago you could see the cairn on the ridge; now you can see twenty metres of heather in every direction, and every direction looks the same. You are sure the path is straight ahead. You are about to find out what "sure" is worth.

Everyone knows that lost people walk in circles, yet until 2009 the belief rested mainly on anecdote.1 Then a team at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tübingen, led by Jan Souman and Marc Ernst, put it to the test. They tracked people with GPS as they tried to walk straight for several hours in the Sahara in Tunisia and in the Bienwald forest in Germany.2 The walkers kept a straight path only when the sun or moon was visible.3 As soon as the sun slipped behind cloud, they started to walk in circles without even noticing.4

Blindfolded, most volunteers walked in circles, some less than 20 metres across.5 The circles had no favourite direction: the same person veered left one time and right the next,6 which sinks the old story that one leg is longer or stronger. The real culprit is noise. Small random errors in the senses that tell you which way you are walking add up over time,7 and your sense of straight ahead quietly drifts. The cure is an outside reference: a tower or mountain in the distance, or the sun.8

Search and rescue researchers have studied what lost people do next. Kenneth Hill described the lost person as one unable to identify or orient their present location with respect to known locations.9 He interviewed rescued people and surveyed 120 deer hunters in Nova Scotia,10 and listed their reorientation strategies, from random travelling and backtracking to climbing for a view and staying put. Robert Koester's International Search and Rescue Incident Database had gathered 50,001 cases by 2007,11 and 91% of them came from the United States.12

concepts.title: In the field: STOP
concepts.contentHtml:
The moment you suspect you are lost, the US Forest Service has a four-letter answer: STOP. Stop, stay calm, stay put; panic is your greatest enemy.1 Then work through the rest before you take another step.

  1. Stop. Sit down, drink something and breathe. Do not move at all until you have a specific reason to take a step.2
  2. Think. Go back over how you got here. What landmarks should you be able to see?
  3. Observe. Get out your compass and work out directions from where you stand. If you are on a trail, stay on it. Following a drainage or stream downhill is a very last resort.3
  4. Plan. Come up with a few plans, think them through, then act on one. If you are not very, very confident of the route, stay put.4 If night is falling, you are injured or you are near exhaustion, stay where you are.5
  5. Hug a tree. Pick an actual tree, a large rock or any fixed point and stay with it.6 Make noise (a whistle is best)7 and leave clues where searchers can see them.8

Why stay? Searchers move faster than you and start from your last known point, and every mile you wander expands the search area enormously, because the area grows with the square of the distance.

Safety Before any walk, tell someone exactly where you are going, your route, when you will be back, what you are driving and where you will park.9 In the UK, if you have a signal, dial 999 or 112 and ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue,10 and do not change your position until the rescue team contacts you.11 Staying put only works if someone knows to look: as the search researcher Robert Koester warns, if no search gets started for you, that is a problem too.12

concepts.title: Myth check: just keep walking
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth If you are lost, pick a direction and keep walking in a straight line; sooner or later you will hit a road.
Reality Without the sun or a distant landmark you cannot hold a straight line, and walking spreads you across an ever bigger search area. When researchers fitted a computer model to real search records, the best-fitting hiker spent over half its time travelling in one direction, the behaviour that carries a lost person furthest.1 Survival chances fall fast, especially if you are not found within the first 51 hours.2 Robert Koester's best advice is to stay put:3 you conserve energy, you do not do anything stupid and you have time to make a shelter and a fire.4
Myth You walk in circles because one leg is longer than the other.
Reality If that were true, each person would always curl the same way. In the Max Planck study the same walker curved left one time and right the next.5 The drift comes from noise in your senses, not your legs.

The most dangerous moment often comes before you admit you are lost. You meet a stream the map does not show and decide the map must be wrong, or that it is some other stream: the trap of bending the map to fit.6 San Diego Mountain Rescue Team's rule is blunt: the ground is right, so stop and back up to the last point where you were certain.7 Koester finds that lost hikers usually keep going when they wrongly think they are still on a trail,8 and that nowadays they often climb in search of a phone signal.9

Wait, really? The Hug-a-Tree programme began with a tragedy. In 1981 nine-year-old Jimmy Beveridge was separated from his family on Palomar Mountain, north-east of San Diego.10 He was found four days later, dead of hypothermia.11 A Border Patrol tracker, Ab Taylor, helped build a programme teaching children to stay with one tree,12 because hypothermia, not hunger or thirst, is what kills lost children.13

title: Reading the Sun
description: Shadow sticks, the watch trick, and the errors hiding in both
tryIt: On a sunny day, push a stick into level ground, mark its shadow tip twice 15 minutes apart, and check your east-west line against a phone compass.

concepts.title: How it works: a clock in the sky
concepts.contentHtml:
Day two. The cloud has lifted, the sun is blazing and you have a straight stick. That is all you need to find north, provided you understand what the shadow is doing.

The Earth spins once a day, so the sun appears to cross the sky from east to west. It does not rise exactly due east or set exactly due west, and the points shift with the seasons. North of the equator the sun stands due south at its highest point; south of the equator that noonday sun marks due north. Shadows move the opposite way to the sun, so in the Northern Hemisphere they swing from west to east and point north at noon.1

Watch the tip of a shadow and you are watching the sun's position printed on the ground. On the two equinoxes, around 20 March and 23 September,2 the sun rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west,3 and the shadow tip of an upright stick follows a straight path from west to east all day, everywhere except the poles.4 On every other day the path curves, which is why the quick shadow methods are approximate.

People have read shadows for a very long time: the sundial is the earliest type of timekeeping device.5 The sun also keeps you walking straight. In the Max Planck experiment, walkers held a course while they could see the sun or moon and lost it under cloud.6 Pacific navigators use the same trick: Nainoa Thompson uses the sun when it is low on the horizon,7 and when the sun gets too high, he steers by the waves.8

concepts.title: In the field: the shadow stick and the watch
concepts.contentHtml:
The US Army's survival manual calls the shadow-tip method simple and accurate.1 You need a straight stick about a metre long and a level spot, free of brush, where it casts a definite shadow.2

  1. Plant the stick. Push it upright into the level ground.
  2. Mark the tip. Put a stone or twig at the end of the shadow. This first mark is always west, everywhere on Earth.3
  3. Wait 10 to 15 minutes. The tip moves a few centimetres.4 Mark its new position: that is east.
  4. Join the marks. A straight line through them is a rough east-west line.
  5. Face north. Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right, and you are facing north,5 in either hemisphere.
  6. For accuracy, take longer. Mark the shadow tip in the morning and use string to scribe an arc through it around the stick. In the afternoon, mark where the lengthening shadow touches the arc again. The line between the two marks is an accurate east-west line.6

No time to wait? Use an analogue watch. North of the equator, hold it flat and point the hour hand at the sun; halfway between the hour hand and 12 lies the north-south line.7 If the watch is on summer time, use 1 instead of 12.8 South of the equator, point 12 at the sun and take the midpoint between 12 and the hour hand.9 With only a digital watch, draw a clock face on paper showing the correct time and use that.10

Safety Never look straight at the sun, even for a moment: work from the shadow, and point the watch hand without staring. The Army is clear that sun methods give only a general direction, so check your line against landmarks before you commit to a long walk on a single reading.

concepts.title: Myth check: the sun rises in the east
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The sun rises due east and sets due west, so you can steer by it at dawn and dusk without a second thought.
Reality It rises exactly east only around the equinoxes.1 For the rest of the year the sunrise point slides back and forth along the horizon, changing fastest at the equinoxes themselves,2 so a midsummer sunrise taken for east sets you off at an angle.
Myth The watch trick works anywhere, at any time.
Reality It assumes your watch shows true local time. The Army says it is accurate only without any changes for daylight saving,3 and that the further you are from the equator, the more accurate it is.4 Clock time and sun time drift apart: the Society for Popular Astronomy notes that during British Summer Time the sun's midday comes at 1 pm,5 and that the Earth's uneven movement around the sun puts it a little ahead of clock time or a little behind.6 The trick also treats the sun as turning evenly around you, and the higher the sun climbs, as it does near the equator, the worse that assumption gets.

Wait, really? The first shadow mark is west everywhere on Earth,7 north or south of the equator, because the sun always crosses from east to west and the shadow always moves the opposite way. What does change is the noon shadow. North of the equator it points north; south of the equator, shadows point south at noon,8 so a traveller who learned the trick in Scotland must flip it in New Zealand.

title: Steering by the Stars
description: Polaris and the Plough, the Southern Cross, and how Pacific navigators read the sky
tryIt: On a clear night, follow the Plough's pointer stars to Polaris, lay two sticks on the ground pointing at it, and check them against a compass in the morning.

concepts.title: How it works: the sky's still point
concepts.contentHtml:
Night falls clear and cold, and the sky is so crowded with stars that the familiar shapes are hard to pick out. Somewhere up there is one star that hardly moves all night.

As the Earth spins, the whole sky seems to wheel anticlockwise around a point in the northern sky.1 By luck, a fairly bright star sits close to that point:2 Polaris, the Pole Star. Because it is almost directly above the North Pole, you can use it like a compass,3 and its angle above the horizon gives you your latitude.4 South of the equator there is no bright star near the south celestial pole, so navigators use patterns that point to it instead.

Pacific navigators turned the whole sky into a compass. Seafarers settled the islands of Remote Oceania 3,500 to 4,000 years ago,5 sailing hundreds and sometimes thousands of kilometres without instruments or charts.6 In 1976 the voyaging canoe7 Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti with Mau Piailug,8 from the island of Satawal in Micronesia, as navigator,9 sensing his way over 2,500 miles.10 He had never been south of the equator, where he could not see the North Star.11

Nainoa Thompson, who learned from Mau, built the Hawaiian star compass on Mau's Micronesian one.12 It divides the horizon into 32 points, each 11.25 degrees from the next,13 and each point is the middle of a "house". A star that rises in a house in the north-east sets in the house of the same name in the north-west,14 so any rising or setting star you recognise is a direction marker. Thompson's crews use about 220 stars, memorising where each one comes up and goes down.15

concepts.title: In the field: north and south by starlight
concepts.contentHtml:
North of the equator you want two patterns, the Plough (the Big Dipper) and Cassiopeia. They sit roughly opposite each other and turn anticlockwise around Polaris,1 so if one is low or hidden the other helps.

  1. Find the Plough. Seven stars in the shape of a saucepan. The two stars forming the outer lip of the pan are the pointers.
  2. Follow the pointers. Draw a line from the bottom pointer through the top one and extend it about five times the gap between them. Polaris sits on that line, a modest star on its own.
  3. Check with Cassiopeia. Its five stars make a W, and Polaris lies between it and the Plough.2
  4. Drop to the horizon. Imagine a line straight down from Polaris to the ground: that point is true north.3 Pick a landmark beneath it.
  5. South of the equator, find the Southern Cross. Its four brightest stars make a tilted cross. Extend the long axis four and a half to five times its length.4 Two pointer stars beside it help you tell the true Cross from the False Cross,5 and the dark patch between them is the Coal Sack.6
  6. Fix it for daylight. Drive stakes into the ground at night pointing the way, so you can travel by them in the morning.
Safety Use the stars to set your direction, not to walk by in the dark: rough ground, drops and water are hard to see at night, so mark the line with stakes and move in daylight. Remember too that Polaris sinks towards the horizon as you travel south, because its height equals your latitude,7 and below the equator it is gone.

concepts.title: Myth check: the brightest star points north
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The North Star is the brightest star in the sky.
Reality People expect it to be very bright, but it is fairly ordinary,1 which is why beginners miss it. Polaris is actually a pulsating supergiant,2 but at 431 light years away it does not look very bright.3 Find it by the pointers, not by its glare.
Myth The Pole Star has always marked north and always will.
Reality The ancient Greeks already knew that Polaris did not mark the pole exactly.4 Earth's axis slowly swings, so the pole star changes: about 5,000 years ago it was Thuban, and in about 5,000 years it will be Alderamin, in Cepheus.5
Myth Marshall Islanders navigated with stick charts as maps.
Reality Nineteenth-century scholars read the lattices of sticks as charts of islands and sailing courses.6 Later studies showed they were teaching devices showing how the main swells run, bend and cross.7 At sea, Marshallese navigators detect the swells by feeling the motion of the canoe.8

Wait, really? In a 2009 study, Captain Korent Joel, one of the last traditional navigators in the Marshall Islands,9 guided a yacht 220 km between two atolls by the old methods.10 Navigators described waves reflected off islands 40 km away, too weak for the scientists11' wave buoy to detect. Birds help too: the noio, a tern, flies out to sea in the morning to fish, ranging about 40 miles, and returns to land at night.12 Ocean-going birds such as the ʻiwa are no use:13 following them will not help you find land.14

title: Map and Compass
description: From lodestone spoons to baseplates: magnetic north, declination and taking a bearing
tryIt: Stroke a sewing needle in one direction with a fridge magnet, float it on a leaf in a bowl of water, and compare the way it settles with a real compass.

concepts.title: How it works: a planet-sized magnet
concepts.contentHtml:
Your phone is dead and the map is soggy, but the little compass on your keyring still swings round and settles. Why should a sliver of steel care where north is?

Because the Earth is a magnet. Its field behaves roughly like a giant bar magnet at the centre of the planet,1 tilted about 9 degrees from the axis the Earth spins on.2 A compass needle simply lines up with the local field,3 and the direction it settles on is magnetic north, which is not quite true north. The pole it points towards also wanders. James Clark Ross located the north magnetic pole in northern Canada in 1831,4 and the most recent survey found it moving north-north-west at about 55 km a year.5

The first compass was probably a spoon.6 Around 60 CE, during China's Han dynasty,7 the writer Wang Chong described a south-pointing spoon that comes to rest pointing south when thrown on the ground.8 Early records describe it as made of lodestone, a naturally magnetic ore, set on a bronze plate marked with directions.9 For a long time it served geomancy, choosing sites and times for buildings and burials, rather than navigation.10 The spoons you see today are twentieth-century replicas built from those descriptions.11

Needles came next. By the 11th century people had noticed that needles rubbed with lodestone also lined up north-south, and they floated them in bowls of water or hung them on silk.12 Chinese scholars also found that needles cooled from red heat while lying north-south became magnetic.13 Early in the 12th century the historian Zhu Yu wrote that pilots steer by the stars at night and the sun by day, and in dark weather look at the south-pointing needle.14 Compasses were in use in Europe by the 12th century.15

concepts.title: In the field: taking a bearing
concepts.contentHtml:
Ordnance Survey reminds walkers that there are three norths.1 True north is the geographic North Pole.2 Grid north is where the grid lines on your map point. Magnetic north is where your compass points.3 A bearing is the direction you need to travel, measured in degrees from north: east is 90, south 180 and west 270.4

  1. Line up your points. Lay the compass on the map with its long edge joining where you are to where you want to go,5 the direction-of-travel arrow pointing at your destination.
  2. Set grid north. Turn the dial until the orienting lines run parallel to the map6's north-south grid lines, with the orienting arrow pointing to the top of the map. Ignore the needle for now.
  3. Allow for the magnet. Apply the grid magnetic angle printed on your map.7 In Great Britain it is small (one OS practice route adds 1 degree),8 but in San Diego County magnetic and true north differ by roughly 11 degrees, and ignoring that drifts you about a mile off course for every five miles walked.
  4. Put red in the shed. Hold the compass flat in front of you and turn your whole body until the red needle lines up with the orienting arrow.9
  5. Walk to a landmark. Look along the direction-of-travel arrow, pick a distinctive tree, rock or peak, walk to it and repeat, rather than staring at the needle as you go.10
Safety Keep the compass away from mobile phones, magnetic buttons, metal belts and the like, which can deflect the needle.11 Rocks can do it too: NOAA warns that local magnetic anomalies exceeding 10 degrees, although rare, do exist,12 and one area of Minnesota has 16 degrees east declination a few miles from 12 degrees west.13 A GPS is useful, but signals drop and batteries fail,14 so carry a map and a compass you know how to use.

concepts.title: Myth check: the needle points to the North Pole
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A compass points at the North Pole.
Reality It points along the local magnetic field. Most of the time, compasses do not point precisely towards the North Pole,1 as the Royal Observatory puts it. The angle between magnetic north and true north is the declination,2 counted as east or west of true north.3 Close to the magnetic poles a compass becomes useless: at the poles themselves the field points straight down and a compass does not show direction at all.4
Myth Magnetic north stays put, so the correction on an old map is good for ever.
Reality The field from Earth's core keeps changing, so the models used to work out declination come with expiry dates,5 and the grid magnetic angle on an Ordnance Survey map is correct only at the time of printing.6

Wait, really? In September 2019, compasses at Greenwich pointed to true north for the first time in about 360 years.7 For the past few hundred years, compass needles in the UK had pointed west of true north.8 The line of zero declination is moving west at around 20 km a year,9 and by 2040 all compasses in the UK will probably point east of true north.10 Greenwich itself had stopped measuring the field long before: in 1926 the electrification of the railways made measurements there impossible, and the instruments moved to Abinger, south of London.11

title: Signposts and Signals
description: Natural clues that work, ones that lie, and how to make rescuers see you
tryIt: In a park or garden, lay out a V about 6 metres long with arms a metre wide using sticks or old towels, then look at it from a hill or a high window.

concepts.title: How it works: reading the land
concepts.contentHtml:
Day five. You have heard every folk trick for finding north without a compass. Some are sound physics; others will march you the wrong way with total confidence. The good ones nearly all come back to the sun.

North of the equator, north-facing slopes get less sun than south-facing ones, so they are cooler and damper.1 In summer they hold on to patches of snow.2 In winter, the trees and open ground on south-facing slopes are the first to lose their snow, and so is the southern side of boulders and large rocks.3 South of the equator, everything flips.4 Wind can help too, but only where there are prevailing directions and you know what they are.

Water and paths are clues to people. Robert Koester's case files show that most lost people, especially injured ones, are found close to a5 linear feature: a stream, a trail, a road, anything you can naturally follow.6 The US Forest Service allows following a drainage or stream downhill, but only as a very last resort: it could lead to a trail or road, and it could also be very dangerous.7

Even houses carry a compass. In Britain, satellite dishes do not point south but towards satellites at about 28 degrees east of south,8 so a street of dishes gives you a rough bearing. And at midday the sun is more or less due south,9 a little later when the clocks are on summer time.

concepts.title: In the field: get found
concepts.contentHtml:
Being found is a job, and you can do it well. The Army's rule is to get your rescuers' attention first and then send a message they understand. Choose the largest clear, flat area on the highest ground you can reach, and make your signals big and geometric, because straight lines and square corners are not found in nature.1

  1. Blow a whistle. Mountain Rescue England and Wales asks for six good long blasts in a minute,2 a minute's pause, then repeat, and not to stop just because you hear a reply, since your blasts may be guiding the team in.3 Whistles have been heard up to 1.6 km away.4
  2. Flash a mirror. On a sunny day a mirror is your best signalling device,5 and pilots have reported seeing flashes up to 160 km away in ideal conditions.6 Catch the glare on your palm, hold up two fingers in a V with the aircraft between them,7 then rock the mirror slowly off your hand and onto the target.8
  3. Write on the ground. Use the ground-to-air code: V for require assistance, X for require medical assistance, N for no, Y for yes and an arrow for proceed in this direction.9 Make each symbol at least 4 m wide and 6 m long with arms 1 m wide,10 in materials that contrast with the ground.
  4. Light it up. In darkness fire is the most effective signal; three fires in a triangle, about 25 m apart, is the international distress signal.11 By day, three columns of smoke say the same.12 Smother a fire with green leaves to make white smoke that shows against dark ground.
  5. Stay with your signals. They mark the spot where rescuers will look for you.
Safety Call 999 or 112 first if you have any signal at all. Never flash a mirror rapidly at an aircraft,13 and do not hold the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds, as it may blind the pilot.14 Build signal fires in a clearing, never in thick woodland, so you do not start a forest fire and endanger yourself.15

concepts.title: Myth check: moss on the north side
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Moss grows on the north side of trees, so every trunk is a compass.
Reality The Army calls the saying inaccurate, because moss grows all the way round some trees.1 Moss grows best in shady spots that are moist or humid.2 North of the equator the north side is usually the shadiest, so moss is most likely there, but not exclusively;3 south of the equator it favours the south side,4 and a damp hollow or a neighbouring tree can put it anywhere.
Myth Tree rings are wider on the sunny side, so a stump points to the equator.
Reality Here the sources disagree. The US Army manuals say growth rings are more widely spaced on the side towards the equator. Tree-ring scientists at the Swiss Federal Institute WSL read lopsided rings differently: wide rings on one side show a tree knocked into a tilt by a landslide or a storm, and a tilted conifer builds compression wood on the underside of its trunk to push itself upright. The Minnesota DNR says rings wider on one side may mean something pushed against the tree as it grew.5 Lean, slope and wind can easily swamp any sunny-side effect.

Wait, really? The moss myth probably began as a genuine way to help people navigate in forests,6 and the Forest Preserve District of Will County, in Illinois, warns that if you let it serve as a map you are likely to get lost.7 Treat every natural clue as one vote, never the deciding one, and check several against the sun or the stars before you set off.
